analysis.one_liner: Requires mortgage companies to try to modify loans before foreclosing on a home.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 2008 during the foreclosure crisis, the bill drew no cosponsors, never received a committee vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required mortgage lenders and loan servicers to work out affordable alternatives before foreclosing on a borrower's main home. It would have barred foreclosure if the company failed to follow those steps, required 60 days' written warning before an adjustable-rate payment jump, banned forcing borrowers into arbitration to get a loan modification, and required free account records. It was sent to the House Financial Services Committee and a housing subcommittee, where hearings were held, but it was never voted on.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners facing default or foreclosure on their primary residence. The bill would have forced lenders to try fee waivers, repayment plans, forbearance, rate or principal modifications, or short refinancing before starting foreclosure, and would have stripped foreclosure rights from lenders that ignored the rules. It also would have given borrowers free access to their loan records and to a live US-based loss mitigation contact.

how_it_helps.text: Requires lenders to pursue loan-preserving steps first — fee waivers, repayment plans, forbearance, and rate or principal modifications — before resorting to short sales or deeds in lieu of foreclosure [S2][S3].
Bars initiating foreclosure on any covered loan if the lender or servicer failed to comply with the loss-mitigation requirements at any time [S2][S3].
Requires written notice of the projected new payment at least 60 days before an adjustable-rate mortgage payment increase [S2][S3].
Prohibits lenders from requiring borrowers to waive claims or agree to arbitration as a condition of receiving a loan modification [S2][S3].
Requires free account documentation on request — payment history, fees, escrow status, and who owns the note — and stops foreclosure while a borrower's written information request is unanswered [S3].
Doubles statutory damages for servicer violations, from $1,000 to $2,000 per violation, and doubles the class-action cap from $500,000 to $1,000,000 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders and loan servicers, who would have absorbed losses from rate cuts, principal forgiveness, and short payoffs, plus the cost of staffing loss-mitigation operations in the United States. Some of those costs could be passed to borrowers through the reasonable fees the bill permits, and lenders argued (as a general matter) that forced modifications raise the cost of mortgage credit.

drawbacks.text: The remedy is blunt: a lender that fails the requirements at any point loses the right to foreclose on that loan entirely, which courts and lenders could have litigated for years [S3].
Lenders could charge a fee for loss-mitigation work, and while the Housing Secretary could strike excessive costs, some added cost would likely flow back to borrowers [S3].

Mandatory modification and short-payoff obligations force lenders to take losses on defaulted loans, which lenders contended would tighten mortgage credit generally — a real cost in a frozen 2008 credit market.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households at risk of losing their homes in 2008, the protections were substantial and directly targeted the servicer practices — lost paperwork, unreachable personnel, forced arbitration, surprise rate resets — that pushed avoidable foreclosures. The main honest cost is to lenders and investors in mortgage loans, whose losses on modifications would have been larger than under voluntary programs, and some of that cost could trickle back into mortgage pricing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which passed it to its housing subcommittee; hearings were held, but the subcommittee or full committee never voted to send it to the House floor, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Maxine Waters introduced the bill on April 2, 2008 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day, with no cosponsors [S4][S5].
On April 16, 2008, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Housing and Community Opportunity, and the subcommittee held hearings [S5].
No further action was recorded before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, so the House never voted on it [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders and servicers avoided a legal duty to modify loans before foreclosing and avoided doubled damages for violations. Homeowners in default got no new federal right to a modification from this bill.

for.name: Rep. Maxine Waters
for.role: Sponsor; member of the House Financial Services Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Barney Frank (D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, routed it to its housing subcommittee, and never reported it out for a House vote

against.name: Rep. Barney Frank
against.what_they_did: As chairman, controlled the committee calendar in 2008 and prioritized the panel's other housing responses; the bill never reached a committee vote

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no roll-call split exists; the sponsor was a Democrat and the Democratic-controlled committee never advanced the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have required them to modify loans, document accounts for free, staff US-based loss mitigation, and face doubled damages, with foreclosure barred when they failed to comply. These duties cut directly against servicer revenue from fees and foreclosure, so the industry's interest in killing the bill ran against borrowers' interest in keeping their homes.
Servicers would have been required to refer any borrower more than 60 days late to a HUD-approved counseling agency, steering borrowers to free help.
